blocks.text: 1.1  The word "hacker" was a compliment once

In the early 1960s, at MIT, the members of the Tech Model Railroad Club spent their nights coaxing the university's first computers into doing things nobody had asked for. They called an elegant, slightly mischievous piece of work a "hack", and the person who pulled it off a "hacker". It was praise. A hack meant you understood the machine better than the people who built it.

The word kept that warm meaning for two decades. The phone phreaks of the 1970s - hobbyists like John Draper, who discovered that a toy whistle from a Cap'n Crunch cereal box sounded at exactly 2600 hertz and could seize control of AT&T's phone lines - were explorers, not thieves. Two of those phreaks, Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs, built and sold "blue boxes" for free phone calls before they built the Apple I. Hacking was curiosity with a soldering iron.

Then the 1980s happened. The film WarGames (1983) showed a teenager nearly starting World War III from his bedroom. And in November 1988 a Cornell student named Robert Tappan Morris released a self-copying program that was meant to measure the size of the internet and instead crashed roughly one in ten of all machines on it - about 6,000 computers. Morris became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Newspaper readers learned one lesson: hacker means criminal. The word never fully recovered.
Sixty years of hacking in one line: the word changed meaning, and a profession grew out of the wreckage.

TRUE STORY.  November 2, 1988. The Morris Worm spread by exploiting three separate flaws, including a debug mode the sendmail authors had left switched on. Its author tried to make it harmless and got the math of reinfection wrong, so machines buckled under dozens of copies. The cleanup cost per machine ran into hundreds of dollars; the internet effectively partitioned itself to survive. It is the founding parable of the whole subject: a small flaw, a large network, and consequences nobody intended.

Out of that wreckage came a strange new job description. If criminals were going to break in anyway, someone had to break in first - politely, with permission, and with a written report. The US Air Force had already run "tiger teams" in the 1970s: friendly attackers hired to test whether classified systems could be breached, so the holes could be closed before a real enemy found them. That idea, friendly attack as a form of defense, is the entire subject of your course.
1.2  What hacking actually is

Strip the folklore away and the definition from your lecture is plain: hacking is gaining unauthorized access to a computer system, network or device in order to manipulate, steal or destroy data, disrupt operations, or do anything else the owner did not agree to.

Notice what the definition does not say. It does not say clever, and it does not say evil. Hacking runs from harmless curiosity (exploring a system to see how it works) to organized crime (ransomware crews that extort hospitals). The act is the same shape in both cases; the intent and the permission are what change. Keep that sentence - it unlocks half the exam.
1.3  Who hackers are

Hackers are the individuals or groups who use technical skill to gain that unauthorized access. That is the whole definition. Their motives scatter across the full range from public service to espionage, which is why the same word carries a positive charge in an engineering lab and a negative one in a courtroom.
1.4  The seven kinds of hacker

Your lecture lists seven types. Do not memorize them as a list; place each one on two axes - did they have permission, and what did they intend? The diagram below does that, and the list then reads itself.
Every hacker type is a point on two axes: permission and intent. The hat language itself comes from old Western films - the hero wore white, the villain black.

Black-hat hackers. Break in without permission, for gain, revenge or harm. They run the cybercrime economy: identity theft, financial fraud, ransomware, denial-of-service attacks. The textbook example is the hacker who breaches a company database to steal customer credit cards.

White-hat hackers. The same skills, run with written permission, to find and fix weaknesses before the black hats find them. Hired as security consultants and penetration testers. This is the career your course is training you for.

Gray-hat hackers. No permission, but no malice either. A gray hat finds a hole, tells the owner, and sometimes asks for a fee. The intention is decent and the act is still illegal in most jurisdictions - including India - because the access itself was unauthorized. Ethics gray, law black and white.

Script kiddies. Beginners who run ready-made tools and scripts written by others, without understanding what the tools do. Individually unsophisticated, but in numbers they still do real damage - a teenager firing a downloaded attack tool at a game server is the standard example.
Hacktivists. Hacking as protest. Website defacements, data leaks and service disruptions in the name of a political or social cause. Supporters call it civil disobedience; the law calls it crime.

State-sponsored hackers. Government operatives or contractors doing espionage, sabotage and cyber warfare against other states. Legal in the eyes of their own government, hostile acts in the eyes of the target. The most resourced attackers on earth.

Cybercriminals. Black hats with a business plan: financially motivated, often organized, running fraud, ransomware and data-theft operations with customer support desks and profit sharing. Crime as an industry.

MEMORY HOOK.  The hat colors come from cowboy films, and the map is two questions: "Were they allowed?" and "What did they want?" White = allowed, helps. Black = not allowed, harms. Gray = not allowed, helps. Every other type is just a black hat with a named motive: money (cybercriminal), politics (hacktivist), government (state-sponsored), or no skill (script kiddie).

TRUE STORY.  In 2010, inspectors found something impossible in Iran's Natanz nuclear facility: uranium centrifuges tearing themselves apart while their control panels reported perfect health. The cause was Stuxnet, a state-built worm that jumped air-gapped networks on USB sticks, hid using stolen digital certificates, and exploited four separate zero-day vulnerabilities. It is the canonical case of state-sponsored hacking: years of work, nation-level funding, and a target picked for geopolitical reasons.
1.5  Ethical hacking, defined properly

Your lecture gives a definition that looks like a contradiction: ethical hacking is an authorized attempt to gain unauthorized access. Read it twice and it stops being a paradox. The access is unauthorized in the technical sense - you attack the system exactly as a criminal would, using their strategies and tools. It is authorized in the legal sense - the owner asked you to, in writing, within agreed limits. Same weapons, opposite mission.

The purpose is always the same: find the security vulnerabilities before a malicious attacker does, so they can be fixed. Two other names for the same work appear in your slides. Penetration testing is the formal, scoped version (Part 3 is devoted to it). Red teaming is the bigger, looser version - a full adversary simulation that may add phishing emails, phone calls and physical break-in attempts on top of the technical attacks, usually without warning the defenders.
And the ethical hacker's mission is the exact opposite of the malicious hacker's: the criminal wants in and stays quiet; the professional gets in, gets out, and writes everything down.
1.6  The code that makes it ethical

Skill does not separate the white hat from the black hat - the tools are identical. What separates them is a code of conduct. Your lecture lists seven principles; together they answer one question: "You can do damage with this knowledge, so why should anyone trust you?"

Legality. Explicit permission from the system owner before any testing, plus compliance with the law of the land. In India the relevant statute is the Information Technology Act, 2000: unauthorized access and data theft are punishable under Sections 43 and 66 regardless of intent. Permission is not a courtesy; it is the whole difference between a test and a crime.

Confidentiality. Anything sensitive you see during a test stays secret. This is why clients make testers sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement - a legal promise not to reveal the vulnerabilities or the data encountered.
Integrity. Honest, complete reporting to the client, and no conflicts of interest. A tester who exaggerates findings to sell more work, or hides them to look good, has failed the job.

Non-malfeasance. Do no harm. Tests are designed to avoid disrupting the business, run in agreed windows, and stop immediately if they put the system at unforeseen risk. Proving a database can be emptied by emptying it is not a test; it is a breach.
Responsibility. You own your actions. Every method must be explainable and justifiable to the client afterwards.
Transparency. Open communication before, during and after: scope, methods, risks, results. No surprises for the system owner.
Professionalism. The threats change monthly, so the learning never stops. A professional who stopped studying in 2015 is a liability with a certificate.

MEMORY HOOK.  Seven principles, one sentence: get permission, keep secrets, tell the truth, break nothing, own your actions, hide nothing, keep learning. If an exam asks "what makes hacking ethical?", the answer is never the tools - it is this code.
1.7  Ethical hacker vs malicious hacker
Your lecturer set this as homework, so treat it as guaranteed exam material. The full model answer is in Part 5; the core of it fits in a table.

rows: Find weaknesses so they can be fixed
Same tools and techniques as the attacker
Careful not to disrupt or damage
Legal - protected by contract and consent

blocks.text: EXAM ALERT.  "How are ethical hackers different than malicious hackers?" is printed as homework on the Lecture 1 slides. The winning one-liner: same skills, opposite mission - one has permission and writes a report, the other has neither.
1.8  The vocabulary every answer needs
Six terms show up in every later lecture. Learn them as one family - they are all answers to "what exactly can go wrong?"
Vulnerability. A weakness in a system - a bug, a misconfiguration, a missing patch, a guessable password. The unlocked window.
Threat. Whatever could exploit that weakness - an attacker, malware, a flood, a careless employee. The burglar walking the street.
Exploit. The actual technique or code that uses a vulnerability to break in. The brick through the window.
Risk. The chance the threat meets the vulnerability, times the damage if it does. Risk is why a flaw on a test server matters less than the same flaw on a bank.
Attack surface. The total of all the places an attacker could try - every open port, page, API and employee. Shrinking it is half of defense.

CIA triad. The three things every attack tries to break: Confidentiality (secrets stay secret), Integrity (data stays correct), Availability (systems stay up). Ransomware hits all three in one move - it reads your files, scrambles them, and takes them away.
MEMORY HOOK.  CIA is the lens: for any attack in any question, ask which of the three letters it breaks. Stealing data = C. Changing data = I. Deleting or blocking = A.
1.9  Kali Linux - the workbench (Lab Assignment 1)

Your first lab assignment asks for an overview of Kali Linux, so here is the story and the substance together. In 2004 a security auditor got tired of installing the same fifty tools on every engagement and built a live CD with everything preloaded. That project became Whoppix, then merged into BackTrack (2006), and was rebuilt on Debian in 2013 as Kali Linux, maintained by the training company Offensive Security. The idea never changed: an entire hacker's workbench on one operating system.

Kali ships with over 600 pre-installed tools, organized by the phases of an attack you will meet in Part 2: information gathering (Dmitry, theHarvester), vulnerability analysis (Nikto, OpenVAS), web application testing (Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP), exploitation (Metasploit, SQLMap), password attacks (John the Ripper, Hydra), wireless attacks, forensics, and reporting. Every tool your four lectures name - Nmap, Nikto, Dmitry, Metasploit, Wireshark - is already in the menu.

Why a whole operating system instead of a few downloads? Three reasons. Everything is preinstalled and version-matched, so a class or a team works on identical setups. It runs as a virtual machine or straight from a USB stick without touching the host machine, so experiments are safe and disposable. And it is free and open source, so the same workbench runs in a student's bedroom and a professional lab.

The flip side is responsibility. Kali is not a toy: every tool in it will happily commit a crime if pointed at a system you do not own. The standing rule of this course - stated on your own slides - is that scanning or attacking anything without written permission is illegal. Keep Kali pointed at your own lab machines and the practice targets your lecturer names.
