sections.title: Part 2 - The Basic Steps of Ethical Hacking

blocks.text: 2.1  Why hacking has a method

Films get hacking wrong in one specific way: they show the break-in and skip the months before it. Real intrusions - the ones that empty databases - look like a heist film, and heist films are honest about the shape of the work. Nobody in a heist film walks into the casino and improvises. They watch the place for weeks, learn the guard rotations, find the weak door, plan the exit, and only then act. The actual theft is the shortest scene.

Ethical hacking copies that shape on purpose, and your lecture calls it the ethical hacking lifecycle: a structured process for finding, exploiting and helping fix vulnerabilities. There are seven phases. A real attacker loops through the first five; the professional adds the two the criminal never does.
The seven-phase lifecycle. Attackers live in phases 1-5; the white hat adds reporting and remediation - which is the entire point of the exercise.
MEMORY HOOK.  Reconnaissance, Scanning, Gaining, Maintaining, Clearing, Reporting, Remediation. Seven words: "Real Spies Gather Maps Carefully, Record Repairs." Say it once, own it forever.
2.2  Phase 1 - Reconnaissance: know the target before you touch it
Objective: collect as much information about the target system, network or organization as possible. This is the casing-the-joint phase, and it comes in two flavors.

Passive reconnaissance gathers information without ever touching the target: public records, WHOIS lookups for the domain, Google Dorking (search-engine tricks that surface exposed files and login pages), Shodan (a search engine for devices on the internet), company websites, employee social media. Nothing is sent to the target, so nothing can be logged. To the target, this phase is invisible.

Active reconnaissance interacts with the target directly: pinging it, scanning for open ports and services. You learn more, but packets arrive at the target and can end up in a log somewhere. More signal, more noise.

Why begin here? Because every later decision is made with this information. You cannot pick an exploit until you know what software is running; you cannot know what is running until you look. Attackers routinely spend most of the total operation time in this phase - the breach itself, when it comes, often takes minutes.
The toolbox for this phase: Nmap, Shodan, Google Dorking, WHOIS, and social engineering. You will meet Dmitry, a dedicated recon tool, in Part 3, where your lecturer uses it for Lab Assignment 3.
2.3  Phase 2 - Scanning: from "what exists" to "what is weak"
Reconnaissance told you what is out there; scanning asks which parts of it are weak. Objective: identify open ports, running services and known vulnerabilities that could be exploited.
Port scanning finds the open ports on the target - the doors that answer when knocked. Part 4 is entirely about this.

Vulnerability scanning checks the discovered services against databases of known weaknesses. Tools like Nessus and OpenVAS automate this: they know tens of thousands of published flaws and test for each.
Network mapping draws the territory: which devices exist, how they connect, where the boundaries are. You cannot defend - or attack - a network you cannot picture.
Tools named in your lecture: Nmap, Nessus, OpenVAS and Nikto. Nikto, the web server scanner, is your Lab Assignment 2 and gets a full walkthrough in section 2.12.
MEMORY HOOK.  Recon vs scanning in one line: reconnaissance asks "what is out there?", scanning asks "where does it hurt?"
2.4  Phase 3 - Gaining access: the break-in

This is the phase films show. A vulnerability found during scanning is located and exploited to enter the system - through a software bug, a misconfiguration, or a weak password. The workhorse tool is Metasploit, a framework that packages thousands of known exploits so the tester can fire a proven attack instead of writing one from scratch. Burp Suite handles web application attacks, SQLMap automates SQL injection, and custom scripts cover whatever is left.

Getting in is usually not enough, because the first foothold is often a limited account. So the phase has a second movement: privilege escalation - climbing from an ordinary user to root (Linux) or administrator (Windows). The root account is the prize because it can read anything, change anything and install anything. Privilege escalation uses local misconfigurations, kernel bugs, weak file permissions or stolen credentials.
2.5  Phase 4 - Maintaining access: staying for the sequel

Once inside, the attacker's problem changes. Getting in was hard; doing it again next week should not be. So attackers install backdoors - hidden ways back into the owned system that survive password changes and reboots: a planted account, a remote access tool, a rootkit that buries itself in the operating system. Metasploit's Meterpreter payload is built for exactly this, and Netcat remains the classic pocket tool for quiet connections.

For an ethical hacker this phase is done in a controlled, documented way - the point is to prove to the client "an attacker could stay here for months" - and every planted mechanism is removed and disclosed at the end. For a criminal, this phase is where the real value lives: a breach that persists for half a year can be milked for half a year. The big breaches you read about usually ran for months before anyone noticed.
2.6  Phase 5 - Clearing tracks: the phase your lecture calls unethical

Your slides are unusually honest here: this phase "is actually an unethical activity". It is the deletion of logs and every other trace of the intrusion - log clearing, removing the tools and scripts that were used, editing audit trails. The goal is that the defenders never learn the breach happened.

Why does an ethical hacking course teach it? Two reasons. First, you cannot detect what you do not understand: a professional who knows how logs get wiped also knows how to protect them - centralized logging, write-once storage, SIEM systems that stream events off the machine in real time so an attacker on the machine cannot reach the evidence. Second, a professional test may check whether the client's monitoring would even notice an intrusion - with permission, and always followed by full disclosure of everything that was done.
MEMORY HOOK.  Phases 3-5 in one line: get in, stay in, clean up. The white hat's version of the same line: get in (carefully), prove it (documented), clean up (everything, disclosed).
2.7  Phase 6 - Reporting: the phase that pays

Here is the entire difference between a white hat and a black hat, written as a job task: document and communicate the findings to the system owner. A penetration test that ends without a report is just a break-in with good intentions.

A real report contains the vulnerabilities discovered, exactly how each was exploited, the level of access gained, the potential business impact, and recommendations for fixing each one. It usually comes in two registers: a technical section for the engineers who will do the fixing, and a plain-language summary for the management who will fund it. Screenshots and proof-of-concept captures go in as evidence - which is why your lab record is built the way it is.
2.8  Phase 7 - Remediation and retesting: close the loop

The last phase belongs to the defenders, with the tester alongside: patch the software, reconfigure the settings, add the missing controls. Then - and this is the part organizations skip at their peril - retest. The same attack is run again against the fixed system to prove the fix actually works. A patch that has not been retested is a hope, not a fix.
The lifecycle then loops: the next scheduled test starts at reconnaissance again, because the system, the threats and the tools have all moved on. Security is a cycle, not a project.
2.9  Why anyone pays for this - the aims of ethical hacking
Your lecture lists seven reasons organizations hire people to attack them. Each maps to a fear every business has:
Identifying vulnerabilities - find the weaknesses before an attacker does. The cheapest time to learn about a hole is from a friend.
Preventing cyber attacks - simulated attacks test whether the defenses actually work, not whether they look good on paper.
Compliance and standards - many industries are legally required to test regularly: PCI-DSS for anyone handling payment cards, HIPAA for US healthcare. Fail the audit, lose the business.
Improving security posture - testing reveals weak network design, vulnerable software and gaps in employee awareness, so fixes go where they matter.
Real-world risk assessment - shows exactly which data and systems an attacker could reach, so the most critical assets get protected first.
Training and awareness - a well-run test teaches the security team more than a year of slides, and builds a culture where people expect attack.
Cost savings - a prevented breach avoids the recovery costs, the legal penalties and the reputational crater. Prevention is cheap in comparison.
2.10  The skills that make an ethical hacker
The lecture slide asks what skills are needed. The honest answer is a stack, from the ground up:
Networking. TCP/IP, ports, protocols, the handshake in Part 4. You cannot attack traffic you cannot read.
Operating systems. Linux fluency above all, plus Windows internals - because those are the targets.
Scripting. Python and Bash, to automate the boring parts and glue tools together.
Web technology. HTTP, databases, how applications are built - because the web is where the holes are.
The tools. Nmap, Metasploit, Burp, Wireshark and the rest of the Kali menu.
Soft skills. Report writing and clear communication - phases 6 and 7 are half the job. And persistence: the work is mostly patient, methodical trying.
2.11  The terminology your examiner loves
The slides end with four terms. Two of them are a homework question, so they get their own diagram.
Footprinting maps the estate; fingerprinting names the occupants. One is passive and broad, the other active and precise.
Footprinting

Footprinting is the part of reconnaissance that gathers every reachable fact about the target: domain names, IP addresses and ranges, namespaces, employee names, phone numbers, email addresses. Think of a footprint in mud: it tells you something big was here, roughly how big, and where it walked. It is mostly passive - assembled from public sources - and it produces the map the rest of the attack is planned on.
Fingerprinting

Fingerprinting - specifically OS fingerprinting - is any method that determines which operating system a remote machine runs. A footprint is broad and shallow; a fingerprint is narrow and exact, like the difference between a shoe print at the door and a fingerprint on the glass. Your slides list the four TCP/IP clues that betray an OS:

TTL (Time-To-Live). The starting value an OS stamps on outbound packets. Linux and macOS start at 64, Windows at 128, most routers and network devices at 255. Read the TTL on a reply and you can often name the family of the sender.
Window size. How much data the OS is willing to receive at once - each TCP stack picks its own defaults.
DF bit. Whether the OS sets the Don't Fragment flag on its packets.
TOS. Whether and how it sets the Type-of-Service field.

Why do these differ at all? Because every operating system's TCP/IP stack was written by a different team making different default choices. Those defaults are as distinctive as handwriting - which is exactly why Nmap can guess an operating system from afar (phase 2 tool, Part 4 feature).
Social engineering

The art of manipulating people instead of machines - using human psychology to gain access to systems, data or personal information. It works because it aims at the one component that cannot be patched: the person. The classic levers are authority ("this is the CEO's office"), urgency ("the server goes down in ten minutes"), fear, and helpfulness. Phishing emails, pretexting phone calls, baited USB sticks in the parking lot, tailgating through a badge door - all the same move in different costumes.

TRUE STORY.  Kevin Mitnick, the most wanted hacker of the 1990s, said later that he rarely broke in through code. He called employees, pretended to be a colleague from another office, and asked. Companies had spent millions on firewalls; the passwords walked out through the help desk. His career is the standing argument that the human layer is the softest one.
Reverse engineering

Backwards engineering: taking a finished product apart to learn how it was made. In security it means disassembling software - often malware - without the source code, to understand what it does, find the vulnerability it uses, or build a defense against it. If footprinting reads the building's exterior, reverse engineering reads its blueprints by taking the bricks out one at a time.
EXAM ALERT.  "Compare footprint vs fingerprint in cyber security" is homework question 3 on your lecturer's post. Part 5 carries the model answer; the diagram above is the one to sketch in the exam.
2.12  Worked example - Nikto (Lab Assignment 2)
The lab asks you to find vulnerabilities on a website using Nikto, a web server scanner that ships with Kali. One command does the work:
nikto -h www.github.com

The -h flag names the host. Nikto then hammers the server with thousands of checks - known vulnerable files, outdated software, dangerous defaults, missing security headers - and prints what it finds. Reading the output from your slide line by line:

"The anti-clickjacking X-Frame-Options header is not present." A security header is missing. Without it, another site can load this page inside an invisible frame and trick users into clicking things they cannot see - clickjacking.
"The X-Content-Type-Options header is not set." The browser may guess a file's type instead of trusting the server, which can turn an uploaded image into executed code. A one-line header prevents it.
"Root page / redirects to https://www.github.com/" - informational: the site pushes visitors to the encrypted version. Good practice, not a flaw.
"No CGI Directories found" - no old-style script folders were detected; you can force a full check with -C all.

Two lessons hide in this small lab. First, "vulnerability" often means "missing one-line safety setting", not a Hollywood exploit. Second, scanners are noisy: a Nikto run is fully visible in the target's logs, which is why it belongs in the scanning phase - after recon, not instead of it. Ctrl+C stops the scan.
MEMORY HOOK.  Scanner ladder to remember: Nikto looks at web servers, Nessus and OpenVAS look at everything, Nmap looks at the network itself.
3.1  From tiger teams to an industry

In the early 1970s the US Air Force had a problem: its computers held classified material, and the only way to know if they were safe was to ask the people who built them - who had every reason to say yes. So it did something smarter. It hired small teams of friendly attackers, gave them permission, and said: break in if you can. These "tiger teams" invented the job your lecturer calls penetration testing.

The logic has not changed in fifty years. Every defense looks solid until someone attacks it, and the first real attack is a terrible time to find out. A penetration test buys the attack in advance, from a friendly attacker, at a scheduled time, with a written report at the end. You are not hoping the walls hold; you are watching someone rattle them.
3.2  The definition, word by word

Your lecture defines penetration testing as "a focused, controlled, and authorized simulation of a cyberattack on a specific system, network, or application to identify and exploit vulnerabilities." Every adjective earns its place:
Focused - it has a scope. Named systems, named dates, named limits. "Test the customer portal in March" is a pentest; "attack anything, forever" is a crime spree.
Controlled - rules of engagement govern it: which techniques are allowed, which systems are off-limits, when to stop. The test must never become the disaster it simulates.
Authorized - written permission from the owner, signed before anything starts. This one word is the legal difference between a consultant and a convict (Part 1, section 1.6).
Simulation - real techniques, real tools, but the goal is proof, not plunder. The tester demonstrates the break-in, documents it, and hands the keys back.

The aim is testing particular assets within an organization - not the whole internet, and not everything the company owns, unless the contract says so. Where ethical hacking is the broad discipline, a pentest is one structured engagement inside it.
3.3  Vulnerabilities and the zero-day

Everything in this field hangs on one object: the vulnerability - the flaw that makes the break-in possible. Most vulnerabilities are known, catalogued, and patchable (each gets a CVE number, a public ID in the global vulnerability database). The frightening kind is the zero-day: a security flaw in software or hardware that attackers are exploiting before the developer even knows it exists.
Why "zero-day": until the vendor learns of the flaw, they have had zero days to write a fix. Everything before that point is undefendable.

The name is a countdown. From the moment the vendor learns about a flaw, a race starts: they write a patch while attackers race to exploit everyone who has not applied it yet. Stuxnet, the state-sponsored worm from Part 1, used four zero-days at once - an unheard-of stockpile that told analysts immediately a government was behind it.

TRUE STORY.  In 2017, Equifax - a company whose entire business is guarding personal data - lost the records of 147 million people. The entry point was a known flaw in Apache Struts, and a patch had been available for two months. Nobody applied it. The breach cost over a billion dollars and the CEO's job. No zero-day, no genius attacker: the most expensive lesson in security history is "apply the patch".
3.4  The five phases of a pentest
Your lecture breaks a pentest into five components. Notice they are the Part 2 lifecycle wearing a suit - the same method, run under contract:
Planning and reconnaissance - define scope and goals, then gather intelligence: network topology, system configurations, software versions. The better the map, the better the test.
Scanning - automated tools sweep the target for known vulnerabilities: misconfigured servers, outdated software, weak passwords. This is where Nikto, Nessus and Nmap earn their keep.

Exploitation - attempt to break in through the identified weaknesses: password cracking, SQL injection, social engineering. Success here answers the only question the client really has: "can someone actually get in?"
Maintaining access - stay inside, the way a real attacker would: plant a backdoor, escalate privileges, show how far the damage could reach - data exfiltration included, simulated and documented.
Analysis and reporting - write it all down: what was exploited, how, what was reached, and what to fix, in language both engineers and management can act on.
3.5  Types by knowledge: black, gray, white box
The first way to classify a pentest is by how much the tester is told beforehand. It is a spectrum, and where you sit on it changes what the test proves.
The knowledge spectrum. Black box simulates the stranger; white box simulates the auditor with the blueprints; gray box sits where most real breaches start - a stolen user account.

Black box testing. The tester knows nothing about the internals - just a company name or a public IP. This simulates an external attacker and is the most realistic rehearsal of an internet-borne attack, but limited time means limited depth. Focus: external vulnerabilities, brute force, social engineering.

White box testing. The tester gets everything: source code, configurations, network layouts. Slow and thorough, it finds the deep flaws - logic errors, bad crypto, insecure defaults - that an outsider would take years to stumble on. Focus: code review, configuration audits, internal vulnerability assessment.

Gray box testing. Partial knowledge - typically a normal user account. This models the two most common real cases: a malicious insider, and an external attacker who phished one password. Focus: what an ordinary account can be turned into.

MEMORY HOOK.  Testing a bank vault: black box - walk in off the street and try. Gray box - open a normal savings account first. White box - the manager hands you the blueprints. Ask which attacker the client is afraid of, and you know which box to use.
3.6  Types by target: where the test points
The second classification is by battlefield. Your lecture names five:
External testing - the perimeter: public IP addresses, firewalls, the company website, anything the internet can touch. The question: "what does the outside world see, and can it get in?"

Internal testing - inside the network, simulating an insider threat or an attacker who already breached the perimeter. Focus: privilege escalation and lateral movement - how far one compromised machine can be turned into ten. Modern defense assumes the perimeter eventually fails, so this test matters most.

Web application testing - one application, deep. The classic findings: SQL injection (tricking the database through an input field), cross-site scripting or XSS (injecting scripts that run in other users' browsers), cross-site request forgery or CSRF (making a logged-in user's browser send requests they never intended), and broken authentication. Input validation and session management are the defenses being measured.
Wireless network testing - Wi-Fi: encryption standards, protocol weaknesses, unauthorized access points. A weak wireless network is a door in the parking lot that bypasses the firewall entirely.
Social engineering testing - the human perimeter: phishing simulations, pretexting calls, baiting, physical entry attempts. Usually the cheapest test to run and the most embarrassing to fail.
3.7  The toolbox
Your lecture names eight tools. Each owns one job in the lifecycle - learn them as specialists, not as a list:

rows: Web application attacks (intercepts and tampers with traffic)
Reading raw network traffic, packet by packet
Web server misconfigurations and known flaws

blocks.text: 3.8  Rules of a professional test
The slides close with best practices, and they read like the ethics code from Part 1 applied to engagements:
Test regularly. Threats evolve monthly; an annual test leaves eleven blind months.
Communicate clearly. Stakeholders should never be surprised by their own test.
Stay legal and ethical. Scope in writing, permission signed, methods agreed.
Cover the whole surface. External, internal, web applications - a strong door beside an open window is still an open window.
Feed findings back. Every test should leave the defenses measurably better; otherwise it was theatre.

Working testers add three habits the slides imply: confirm backups exist before touching production, avoid denial-of-service tests on live systems unless the client explicitly accepts the risk, and agree an emergency stop contact before the first packet.
3.9  Worked example - Dmitry (Lab Assignment 3)

Lab 3 is reconnaissance with Dmitry, the Deepmagic Information Gathering Tool - a small, fast passive-recon program on the Kali menu. Passive is the point: most of what Dmitry collects comes from public sources, so the target sees nothing.
The flags, one line each:

rows: Save output to a file (default %host.txt, or the file you name)
Whois lookup on the host's IP address
Whois lookup on the domain name
Pull Netcraft.com information on the host (hosting history, OS hints)
TCP port scan on the host
Port scan that also reports filtered ports
Read the banner each scanned port sends back

blocks.text: The lab then walks a real sequence against google.com:
dmitry -w www.google.com        # whois on the domain: registrar, dates, contacts
dmitry -i 172.217.31.196       # whois on the IP: which network block owns it
dmitry -s www.google.com       # subdomains: mail.google.com, docs.google.com, ...
dmitry -e www.google.com       # email addresses exposed on public pages
dmitry -n www.google.com       # Netcraft: hosting provider, OS, uptime
dmitry -wsepn www.google.com   # flags combine - five reports from one command
The Lab Assignment 3 command sequence, with what each line actually pulls.

Read that sequence as a story about one company: who registered the domain and when (-w), whose network it lives on (-i), what other doors exist (-s), which employees are exposed (-e), and what the infrastructure looks like (-n). That dossier, assembled without sending a single suspicious packet to the target, is phase 1 done properly - and it is why "multiple flags at a time" exists: reconnaissance is gathering, so you gather everything in one pass.

MEMORY HOOK.  Dmitry in one breath: -w who owns it, -i whose network, -s what doors, -e which people, -n whose servers, -p which ports answer, -b what the ports say, -f even the shy ports, -o save it all.
3.10  Pentest or vulnerability assessment - know the difference

A distinction examiners and interviewers both love. A vulnerability assessment finds and lists weaknesses - a prioritized inventory of holes, usually scanner-driven. A penetration test goes further: it exploits the holes to prove what an attacker could actually do with them. Assessment says "your window is unlocked"; the pentest climbs through it (with permission) and photographs the jewelry. Assessments are broader and cheaper; pentests are narrower, deeper and more convincing.

EXAM ALERT.  "What is the difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test?" is the most common theory question in this subject, and the one-line answer is: a vulnerability assessment lists the holes; a penetration test proves them.
4.1  The tool that outlived its era

In September 1997, a hacker named Fyodor (Gordon Lyon) published an article in Phrack - the underground's oldest e-zine - titled "The Art of Port Scanning", with source code attached. The program was Nmap: the Network Mapper. It was free, it was better than the commercial scanners, and it stayed free. Twenty-eight years later it is still the first tool reached for by network administrators taking inventory, and by attackers doing reconnaissance - the same binary, the same commands, serving both.

TRUE STORY.  In The Matrix Reloaded (2003), Trinity needs to disable a power grid. She sits at a terminal and runs a real tool, nmap, finds SSH on port 22, and exploits it. Security people nearly cheered in the cinema: it was the first time Hollywood showed hacking with actual software instead of flying through glowing tunnels. The scene made Nmap famous far outside the field.
4.2  First, understand the map - IP addresses and ports

Nmap answers questions about a landscape, so learn the landscape first. Two addressing systems stack on top of each other. The IP address finds the machine - one building among billions. But a single machine runs dozens of services at once: a web server, a mail server, a database, remote login. Traffic for each has to reach the right program. That is what ports are for.

Your lecture's definition: a port is a virtual point where network connections start and end. Ports are software-based, managed by the operating system, and each port belongs to one process or service. The apartment-building analogy holds up well: the IP address is the street address of the building; the port number is the apartment door.
One IP address, many services. The address finds the building; the port number finds the door.
Port numbers run from 0 to 65535, and they are standardized across all network devices so that everyone agrees which service lives behind which number. Three bands matter:

rows: The famous services: HTTP on 80, HTTPS on 443, SSH on 22. Reserved by convention.
Claimed by specific applications: MySQL on 3306, RDP on 3389.
Temporary ports your own machine picks when it makes an outgoing connection.

blocks.text: The well-known twenty you will meet again and again:

rows: the front door of the web

blocks.text: MEMORY HOOK.  Port mnemonics that survive exam stress: 22 = SSH ("2-2, the secure crew"), 23 = Telnet (one more than secure, one step less safe), 80 vs 443 = the web, unlocked vs locked. And 3306 for MySQL is worth brute memorization - it appears in every database question.
4.3  The handshake every scanner exploits

Before two machines talk over TCP, they introduce themselves with the three-way handshake. It exists because both sides need to confirm they can send and receive, and agree on starting sequence numbers for the conversation:
Left: the full three-way handshake a normal connection performs. Right: the SYN scan - the scanner learns the port is open from the SYN-ACK, then walks away with an RST before any connection exists.
SYN - the client says "let us talk" and proposes a starting sequence number.
SYN-ACK - the server answers "agreed" and proposes its own.
ACK - the client confirms. The channel is open; applications on both sides can now see and log the connection.

Now the clever part, and the reason this belongs in an Nmap lecture. A basic connect scan finishes the handshake with every port - reliable, but every completed connection can be logged by the application. The SYN scan (also called the half-open scan, nmap -sS) sends the SYN, reads the SYN-ACK - which already answers the only question, "is this port open?" - and then sends RST to abort before the handshake completes. No connection, so older systems and many applications log nothing. It is a prank call: ring once, learn someone is home, hang up. This is why the SYN scan is the default and the most popular scan type in the world.
4.4  The three answers a port can give
Every port Nmap probes answers in one of three states, and your lecture defines all three:
Open - a service is listening and accepts connections. This is the finding: every open port is a possible way in, and every one should have a reason to exist.
Closed - the machine answers but nothing is listening; the OS replies with a refusal (a RST packet). Not exploitable right now, but the machine itself is alive and reachable - useful intelligence.

Filtered - a firewall is in the way. It silently drops the probe (or sends a polite rejection), so Nmap cannot tell whether the port behind it is open or closed. Filtered ports are why scans slow down: Nmap must retry before giving up.

MEMORY HOOK.  The doorman model: open = the door opens. Closed = "nobody lives here", said from inside. Filtered = a guard who pretends you do not exist. Attackers love the first, note the second, and curse the third.
4.5  What Nmap can do
The lecture lists the features; here is each one with the reason it exists:

Host discovery. Which devices on this network are even alive? Nmap can run a ping sweep - pinging a range of IP addresses to see which answer - mapping the population of a network in seconds. (Your slides define this term explicitly; expect it as a short answer.)
Port scanning. The core trick: probe a range of ports on a range of hosts and report which are open, closed or filtered, and which service is answering on each.

Service and version detection (-sV). Nmap does not just find port 80 open - it asks the service who it is: "Apache httpd 2.4.49". Version numbers matter because vulnerabilities attach to versions: a known flaw in Apache 2.4.49 is a known way in, the moment the version is known.

Operating system detection (-O). OS fingerprinting, exactly as Part 2 described it: Nmap reads the TTL, window size, DF bit and TOS habits in the replies and matches them against a database of known stacks. Different OS families choose different defaults - their network handwriting gives them away.

NSE - the Nmap Scripting Engine. Hundreds of ready-made scripts turn the scanner into a specialist: vulnerability detection (--script vuln), advanced service discovery, brute-force checks against specific services. You can also write your own. This is the feature that keeps a 1997 tool modern.
Network mapping. From the scan data, Nmap builds the picture of the network: devices, their relationships, their open doors. The deliverable of phases 1 and 2, in one diagram.
Stealth scanning. SYN half-open scans, UDP scans, timing controls (paranoid-slow to insane-fast) that trade speed for invisibility to firewalls and intrusion detection systems.
Customizability. Scan one port or all 65535, one host or a whole subnet, fast or quiet - every knob is on the command line, which is why the next section exists.
4.6  Where Nmap gets used
Five use cases from your lecture, and note how each one is a phase or an aim from earlier lectures with Nmap as the instrument:
Network inventory - discover every device and service, and write down what the network actually contains (versus what the documentation claims).
Vulnerability assessment - find the open ports and old versions that should not be there, feeding the scanners from Part 3.
Penetration testing - the reconnaissance and scanning engine of the whole Part 3 process.
Compliance audits - prove that open ports match the security policy: nothing exposed that the rules forbid.
Troubleshooting - "is the service even listening?" is the first question in any outage, and Nmap answers it from the outside.
4.7  The command line, piece by piece (Lab Assignment 4)

Lab 4 gives twelve commands. Here is each one with what it does and when you would reach for it. The pattern to internalize: nmap [options] [target], where the target can be a name, an IP, or a whole subnet.
nmap -h
1. Help. Every option Nmap knows, printed. When in doubt, ask the tool.
nmap testphp.vulweb.com
2. The default scan: the 1000 most common ports on a target. This is "knock on the usual doors". testphp.vulweb.com is a deliberately vulnerable practice site - scanning it is legal by design.
nmap -F testphp.vulweb.com
3-4. -F = Fast: only the 100 most common ports. When you want a quick answer - "is there obviously something exposed?" - this is the one. Works on names and IPs alike.
nmap -p mysql,https,ftp 199.59.243.227
5-9. -p picks the ports: one port, a comma list, a range, mixed ranges - and, when you forget numbers, service names (mysql, https, ftp). The shape of -p is: exact, listed, ranged, or named.
nmap -A www.gmail.com

10. -A = Aggressive: OS detection, version detection, script scanning and traceroute in one flag. Loud and slow - the full interview, not a knock. Use it when stealth does not matter and information does.

11. Subnet scan: the /24 means "all 256 addresses in this block" - every device on your local network. This is the ping sweep from section 4.5 in one line, and the standard first command on any new network.
12. -O = OS detection: guess the operating system from its TCP/IP fingerprint (the TTL / window size / DF / TOS handwriting from Part 2). Usually needs root privileges.
Five flags the lab does not list but professionals use daily:

rows: The SYN half-open stealth scan from section 4.3 - the professional default
Version detection: not just "80 open" but "Apache 2.4.49"
All 65535 ports, not just the common ones - slow but complete
Faster timing (T0 paranoid to T5 insane) - T4 is the normal impatient choice
Save the results to a file - because a scan you cannot show is a scan you cannot report

blocks.text: MEMORY HOOK.  Command anatomy in one line: nmap tells you the machine, -p picks the doors, -F makes it quick, -A makes it thorough, -O names the operating system, -sV names the software, /24 names the whole street.
4.8  Reading an Nmap report
Exam questions love to show a scan result and ask what it means. A typical aggressive scan report reads like this (representative output against a practice host):
# nmap -A scanme.nmap.org
Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for scanme.nmap.org (45.33.32.156)
Host is up (0.21s latency).
Not shown: 996 closed tcp ports (reset)
PORT    STATE    SERVICE  VERSION
22/tcp  open     ssh      OpenSSH 6.6.1p1 (protocol 2.0)
80/tcp  open     http     Apache httpd 2.4.7
9929/tcp open    nping-echo Nping echo
OS details: Linux 3.2 - 4.9
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 21.4 seconds
A representative -A report. Learn to read it line by line - it compresses everything in this part.
"Host is up" - host discovery succeeded: the machine is alive and answering.
"Not shown: 996 closed tcp ports" - Nmap hides the boring majority. 996 doors answered "nobody here"; only the interesting ones are printed.

The PORT table - the deliverable: port, state, service name, and version. 22/open/ssh means remote login is possible; 80/open/Apache 2.4.7 names the exact web server, which an attacker (or auditor) can now check against the vulnerability databases from Part 3.
"OS details: Linux" - the -O fingerprint at work.
The final line - scope and cost: one host, 21 seconds. Multiply by a /24 subnet and you see why -F exists.
4.9  The law of the scan

Your slides end the Nmap lecture with a warning, and it deserves its own section because students underestimate it: scanning networks without authorization is illegal and unethical, full stop. In India, unauthorized scanning and access fall under the Information Technology Act, 2000. "I was only looking" is not a defense, and scan traffic is unmistakable in server logs.

The good news is that practice targets exist precisely so you never have an excuse: scanme.nmap.org is operated by the Nmap project itself, explicitly for scanning practice, and testphp.vulweb.com (from your lab) is a deliberately vulnerable site built to be attacked. Add your own virtual machines and you have a full legal shooting range. The rule from Part 1 has not changed since section 1.6: permission first, always.

EXAM ALERT.  Expect a short question here: "Is port scanning legal?" Answer: only with authorization - the same action is a professional service with permission and a punishable offence without it (IT Act 2000). Practice targets like scanme.nmap.org exist for exactly this reason.
Thirty lines. If the exam starts in an hour, read this page and nothing else.
1. Hacking = unauthorized access to systems or data, for anything from curiosity to crime.
2. Hacker types sit on two axes: permission and intent. White = yes + help. Black = no + harm. Gray = no + help.
3. Script kiddie = unskilled, runs others' tools. Hacktivist = political motive. State-sponsored = government. Cybercriminal = organized money.
4. Ethical hacking = an authorized attempt to gain unauthorized access. Also called penetration testing or red teaming.
5. The ethics code: permission, confidentiality (NDA), honesty, do no harm, responsibility, transparency, keep learning.
6. Same tools, opposite mission: the white hat's report is the difference between a profession and a crime.
7. CIA triad: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. Every attack breaks at least one letter.
8. Vulnerability = weakness. Threat = what could abuse it. Exploit = the technique that does. Risk = likelihood x damage.
9. Lifecycle (7): Reconnaissance, Scanning, Gaining access, Maintaining access, Clearing tracks, Reporting, Remediation + retesting.
10. Mnemonic: Real Spies Gather Maps Carefully, Record Repairs.
11. Recon: passive (WHOIS, Shodan, Google dorking - invisible) vs active (probing - visible in logs).
12. Scanning finds open ports, services, known vulnerabilities: Nmap, Nessus, OpenVAS, Nikto.
13. Gaining access = exploitation, mainly Metasploit; then privilege escalation to root/admin.
14. Maintaining access = backdoors (Meterpreter, Netcat, rootkits). Clearing tracks = deleting logs - the unethical phase.
15. Reporting is the deliverable. Retesting proves the patch works. A fix without retest is a hope.
16. Footprinting = broad map of the estate (domains, IPs, employees) - passive. Fingerprinting = exact OS/service identity - active.
17. OS fingerprinting reads TTL (Linux 64, Windows 128, devices 255), window size, DF bit, TOS.
18. Social engineering = hacking the human: authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness. Cannot be patched.
19. Reverse engineering = taking finished software apart to understand it - malware analysis lives here.
20. Pentest = focused, controlled, authorized simulation of a cyberattack. Vulnerability assessment lists holes; a pentest proves them.
21. Zero-day = exploited before the vendor knows - zero days to fix. Stuxnet burned four; Equifax fell to a two-month-old patch.
22. Box types by knowledge: black (nothing, external stranger), gray (partial, insider/stolen login), white (everything, code + configs).
23. Pentest targets: external, internal, web app (SQLi, XSS, CSRF), wireless, social engineering.
24. Port = virtual connection endpoint per service. 0-1023 well-known, 1024-49151 registered, 49152-65535 dynamic.
25. Ports to own: 21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 445 SMB, 3306 MySQL, 3389 RDP.
26. Port states: open (listening), closed (alive, nothing listening), filtered (firewall hiding it).
27. Three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. SYN scan sends RST instead of the ACK - half-open, quieter.
28. Nmap features: host discovery (ping sweep), port scan, version detection -sV, OS detection -O, scripts (NSE), stealth -sS.
29. Nmap lab: default = 1000 ports, -F = 100 fast, -p exact/list/range/name, -A aggressive, /24 whole subnet, -O the OS.
30. Dmitry (recon): -w domain whois, -i IP whois, -s subdomains, -e emails, -n Netcraft, -p ports, -b banners, -o save. Flags combine: -wsepn.
31. Nikto -h <host> scans a web server for missing headers and known flaws; noisy, shows in logs.
32. Legality: no scan or attack without written authorization (IT Act 2000). Practice on scanme.nmap.org and testphp.vulweb.com.
Good luck tomorrow. Walk in knowing the lifecycle, the three homework answers, and the port table - those three alone cover most of the marks.

questions.question: How are information, cyber security and network security interrelated?
questions.answer:
The three terms describe the same mission at three different sizes, and the cleanest way to see it is as nesting boxes, widest to narrowest.

Information security is the widest box: protecting information in every form it takes - on paper, spoken aloud, on a laptop, on a backup tape, in an employee's memory. Its tools include locked filing cabinets and shredders as much as encryption. Its goal is the CIA triad applied to all information: confidentiality, integrity, availability.

Cyber security sits inside it: protecting the digital subset - computers, servers, phones, applications, and the data stored on them - against attack. Everything cyber security protects is information, but it is specifically information inside digital systems, and the threats are digital ones: malware, intrusions, phishing.

Network security is the innermost box: the part of cyber security that guards data while it moves between systems - firewalls, intrusion detection, Wi-Fi encryption, router configuration. A firewall rule is network security; it protects the network so that the systems can be protected, so that the information can be protected.

So the relationship is containment and dependence: network security is one layer of cyber security, and cyber security is one layer of information security. A breach at any inner layer endangers every layer above it - an open network lets attackers reach the systems, and compromised systems give up the information.

The nesting answer: network security sits inside cyber security, which sits inside information security. Sketch this in the exam and the question answers itself.

questions.question: How are ethical hackers different from malicious hackers?
questions.answer:
The shortest true answer: same skills, opposite mission. Both study systems for weaknesses, and both use the same tools - Nmap, Metasploit, Burp Suite. Everything else diverges.

An ethical hacker works with written permission from the system owner, inside an agreed scope, taking care not to disrupt operations. A malicious hacker has no permission and recognizes no scope. The ethical hacker's goal is to find vulnerabilities so they can be fixed; the malicious hacker's goal is to exploit them for theft, extortion, espionage or damage. During the work, the professional avoids harm (non-malfeasance); the criminal causes it. And afterwards comes the sharpest difference of all: the ethical hacker writes a detailed report and helps remediate, while the malicious hacker clears logs and installs backdoors to return later.

Legally, the difference is total: authorized testing is a legitimate, well-paid profession protected by contract, while unauthorized access is a criminal offence - in India under the Information Technology Act, 2000. One sentence to close any exam answer: the difference is not the technique, it is the consent, the intent, and the report.

questions.question: Compare footprint vs fingerprint in cyber security.
questions.answer:
Both are reconnaissance terms, and they differ in scope, depth and method - the diagram in Part 2 is worth redrawing in the exam.

Footprinting is the broad mapping of a target organization, done early and mostly passively: domain names, IP ranges, subdomains, employee names, email addresses, phone numbers - the whole estate, sketched from public sources. It answers "how big is the target and where are its edges?", and because it touches nothing, the target notices nothing.

Fingerprinting is narrow and exact: identifying precisely what is running on one machine - the operating system and its version, or the exact software behind a port. It works by reading the target's technical habits: TTL values (Linux starts at 64, Windows at 128, network devices at 255), TCP window size, the DF bit, TOS fields. It is active - packets are sent and replies are measured.

The analogy holds the comparison together: a footprint tells you something big passed through and roughly where it went; a fingerprint tells you exactly who it was. Footprinting maps the estate; fingerprinting names the occupants.

questions.question: Define hacking.
questions.answer: Gaining unauthorized access to systems, networks or devices to manipulate, steal or destroy data, or disrupt operations.

questions.question: What is ethical hacking?
questions.answer: An authorized attempt to break into a system using attacker techniques, so vulnerabilities can be fixed before criminals find them.

questions.question: Name two other terms for ethical hacking.
questions.answer: Penetration testing and red teaming.

questions.question: What separates a white hat from a black hat if the tools are the same?
questions.answer: Permission, intent, and the report - consent, purpose, disclosure.

questions.question: What is a gray-hat hacker?
questions.answer: One who breaks in without permission but without malice, usually reporting the flaw afterwards - still illegal.

questions.question: What is a script kiddie?
questions.answer: An unskilled attacker running tools written by others without understanding them.

questions.question: What do hacktivists hack for?
questions.answer: Political or social causes - protest through defacement, leaks and disruption.

questions.question: What does CIA stand for in security?
questions.answer: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.

questions.question: What is a vulnerability? A threat? An exploit?
questions.answer: A weakness; whatever could abuse it; the technique that actually does.

questions.question: List the seven phases of the ethical hacking lifecycle.
questions.answer: Reconnaissance, scanning, gaining access, maintaining access, clearing tracks, reporting, remediation and retesting.

questions.question: Which phase distinguishes the professional from the criminal?
questions.answer: Reporting (phase 6).

questions.question: What is the difference between passive and active reconnaissance?
questions.answer: Passive never touches the target and is invisible; active interacts with it and can be logged.

questions.question: Name the primary tool for the gaining-access phase.
questions.answer: Metasploit.

questions.question: What is privilege escalation?
questions.answer: Climbing from a limited account to root/administrator after getting in.

questions.question: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
questions.answer: A flaw exploited before the developer knows of it - the vendor has had zero days to fix it.

questions.question: What is a port?
questions.answer: A virtual endpoint for network connections, software-based, managed by the OS, tied to one service.

questions.question: How many ports exist per machine, and which band holds the famous services?
questions.answer: 0-65535; the well-known ports are 0-1023.

questions.question: Name the three port states.
questions.answer: Open, closed, filtered.

questions.question: What is a ping sweep?
questions.answer: Pinging a range of IP addresses to discover which devices on a network are alive.

questions.question: What does NSE stand for?
questions.answer: The Nmap Scripting Engine - scripts that add vulnerability detection and advanced discovery to Nmap.

questions.question: Why did the word "hacker" change meaning?
questions.answer: It began as praise at 1960s MIT for clever, playful programming. The 1988 Morris Worm, which crashed about a tenth of the internet and led to the first conviction under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, fixed the word's criminal meaning in the press and the public mind. The older meaning survives inside engineering culture, but the legal and media meaning is the criminal one.

questions.question: Explain "an authorized attempt to gain unauthorized access".
questions.answer: The access is unauthorized in the technical sense: the tester breaks in exactly as an attacker would, without being let in. It is authorized in the legal sense: the owner gave written permission first. The phrase compresses the whole profession into one paradox - attack the system as its enemy, with its blessing.

questions.question: Why is confidentiality enforced through NDAs in penetration testing?
questions.answer: A tester routinely sees the client's weakest points and sometimes sensitive data while proving access. Publishing or misusing any of it would hand attackers a map. The Non-Disclosure Agreement turns that professional duty into a legal one, binding the tester to silence about findings and data.

questions.question: Why does scanning come after reconnaissance rather than before?
questions.answer: Scanning sends packets to the target, which costs stealth and can trigger alarms. Reconnaissance first narrows the target list from public sources, so the noisy scanning phase hits only what matters. Look silently, then knock - never knock on every door in the city.

questions.question: Why do attackers install backdoors instead of just stealing data immediately?
questions.answer: Because persistent access is worth more than a single raid. Re-exploiting a patched hole may be impossible, so a backdoor - a planted account, a remote-access tool, a rootkit - guarantees re-entry after passwords change and systems reboot. Most major breaches ran for months before discovery precisely because of this phase.

questions.question: Your lecture calls clearing tracks "an unethical activity". Why teach it anyway?
questions.answer: Defenders cannot protect what they do not understand. Knowing how attackers wipe logs teaches professionals to centralize logging and stream events off the machine in real time, out of the attacker's reach. It also lets a tester check - with permission - whether the client's monitoring would even notice an intrusion.

questions.question: Black box vs white box testing - which finds more bugs, and which is more realistic?
questions.answer: White box finds more, because full knowledge - source code, configurations, diagrams - lets the tester audit deeply instead of probing blindly. Black box is more realistic, because it rehearses exactly what an outside attacker with zero knowledge would face. Mature programs run both: realism from black box, depth from white box.

questions.question: Why is internal penetration testing taken so seriously now?
questions.answer: Modern defense assumes the perimeter eventually fails - one phished password and the attacker is inside. Internal testing measures the blast radius of that moment: privilege escalation and lateral movement from an ordinary foothold. A network that is hard outside and soft inside is a coconut; attackers love coconuts.

questions.question: Why does service version detection matter so much to an attacker?
questions.answer: Vulnerabilities attach to versions. "Port 80 is open" is a fact; "port 80 runs Apache 2.4.49" is a plan, because known flaws are catalogued by software version. Version detection converts a map into a menu of exploits.

questions.question: What makes the SYN scan stealthier than a full connect scan?
questions.answer: The connect scan completes the three-way handshake, creating a real connection the application can log. The SYN scan reads the server's SYN-ACK - which already reveals the port is open - and aborts with RST before the handshake finishes. No connection means far less to log.

questions.question: A port comes back "filtered". What does that tell you, and what does it hide?
questions.answer: A firewall or filter is dropping or rejecting the probes, so Nmap cannot learn whether the port behind it is open or closed. It tells you the network is defended and that the admin thinks about security. It hides exactly the information you wanted - which is the point of the firewall.

questions.question: Why do organizations pay to be attacked?
questions.answer: Because a friendly attack is the cheapest way to learn the truth: it finds holes before criminals do, tests whether defenses actually work, satisfies compliance rules like PCI-DSS, and costs a fraction of a real breach. Every phase of a real intrusion, minus the damage, plus a report.

questions.question: Why is social engineering called "hacking the human"?
questions.answer: It targets the one component that cannot be patched: people. Authority, urgency, fear and helpfulness are exploited to make employees hand over access willingly. Kevin Mitnick's career showed that asking for a password often beats cracking one.

questions.question: What is the difference between a vulnerability assessment and a penetration test?
questions.answer: A vulnerability assessment finds, lists and prioritizes weaknesses - broad, mostly automated, no exploitation. A penetration test goes further and exploits selected weaknesses to prove real impact. The assessment says the window is unlocked; the pentest climbs through it, with permission, and takes a photo.

questions.question: Why does ethical hacking exist as a profession at all?
questions.answer: Because defenses cannot be trusted until they are attacked, and the first real attack is the worst possible time to test them. The 1970s tiger teams discovered that the only honest measure of a system's security was a skilled, friendly adversary. Ethical hacking buys the attack in advance, from someone who will hand the keys back and write down how they got in.

questions.question: Why is written permission - not skill, not intent - the legal line between a professional and a criminal?
questions.answer: Because intent is invisible and skill is neutral; the law can only judge observable facts. Unauthorized access is an offence under laws like India's IT Act 2000 regardless of how noble the motive - a gray hat proving a point commits the same act as a black hat committing a theft. The signed authorization is what converts identical keystrokes from crime into service.

questions.question: Why do OSes betray themselves through TTL values?
questions.answer: Each operating system's TCP/IP stack was written by a different team that picked its own defaults: Linux starts TTL at 64, Windows at 128, network gear at 255. Every router hop subtracts one, so the received value reveals the starting value. Defaults chosen decades ago, never changed, now act as handwriting - which is what OS fingerprinting reads.

questions.question: Why is phase 6, reporting, "the phase that pays"?
questions.answer: Because the client's money does not buy the break-in - it buys the knowledge of the break-in. A pentest without a report leaves the holes open and the client ignorant, which makes it indistinguishable from espionage. The report converts an attack into a fix list, and that conversion is the entire product.

questions.question: Why must remediation be followed by retesting?
questions.answer: Because an untested fix is a hope. Patches get misapplied, configurations revert, and fixes sometimes open new holes. Retesting reruns the original attack against the repaired system, turning "we believe it is fixed" into "we watched the attack fail".

questions.question: Why does a hacker need a structured lifecycle at all - why not just attack?
questions.answer: Because unstructured attacks are inefficient and noisy: random exploitation triggers alarms while missing the actual weakness. The lifecycle front-loads silent information gathering so that the noisy phases are short, targeted and purposeful. Heist films get this right - the crew that plans for weeks acts for minutes.

questions.question: Why is "do no harm" technically hard during a real pentest?
questions.answer: Because the test uses real attacks against real systems. An exploit can crash a fragile service; a password spray can lock accounts; a scan can saturate an old firewall. Professionals manage this with rules of engagement: agreed windows, excluded systems, rate limits, and an emergency stop contact. Proving a system can fall over by pushing it over is a failure of the test, not a success.

questions.question: Why did Stuxnet's four zero-days reveal a government behind it?
questions.answer: Zero-days are rare and expensive - each represents months of research or six figures on the exploit market, and each burns forever once used. Spending four on a single operation meant an attacker with nation-level resources and a target worth that price: Iran's nuclear program. Ordinary criminals hoard zero-days; only states spend them like that.

questions.question: Why can't a firewall make Nmap useless?
questions.answer: A firewall can only make ports filtered - it hides their state but not the machine's existence, and Nmap still maps what the filter does protect, revealing the firewall's own rules by their shadows. Misconfigured firewalls leak ports; perfectly configured ones still leave the services that must be public - like the web server - visible and testable. Defense in depth exists precisely because one wall is never enough.

questions.question: Why is the human layer called "the unpatched vulnerability"?
questions.answer:
Software gets security updates; people do not. The same psychological levers - authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness - work in 2026 exactly as they did in 1990, on almost every employee, almost every time. That is why social engineering testing is a standard pentest type and why the strongest technical defenses still lose to one well-crafted phone call.

These are written the way a full-mark answer is built: definition, structure, detail, close. Match the shape and the marks follow.

questions.question: Describe the seven phases of the ethical hacking lifecycle with the objective of each.
questions.answer:
Open with the definition: the lifecycle is the structured process ethical hackers follow to identify, exploit and help fix vulnerabilities, mirroring how real attackers work. Then walk the seven phases, one or two lines each.

Reconnaissance gathers maximum information about the target, passively (WHOIS, social media, Google dorking - invisible to the target) and actively (direct probing). Scanning turns that knowledge into weaknesses: open ports, running services, known vulnerabilities, and a map of the network, using Nmap, Nessus, OpenVAS, Nikto. Gaining access exploits a discovered weakness - a bug, a misconfiguration, a weak password - usually with Metasploit, followed by privilege escalation to root or administrator. Maintaining access installs backdoors so the tester can prove persistence, the way a criminal would return at will. Clearing tracks removes logs and artifacts; the lecture itself notes this is the unethical phase, taught so defenders learn to protect their logs. Reporting documents every finding, exploit path, access level and recommendation - the deliverable that separates the professional from the criminal. Remediation and retesting work with the security team to patch and then re-attack the fix to prove it holds.

Close with the shape of the whole: attackers loop phases one to five; ethical hackers add six and seven, and those two phases are the entire commercial product.

questions.question: Explain the different types of hackers with examples.
questions.answer:
Frame first: every hacker type is fixed by two questions - do they have permission, and what is their intent? Then the list.

Black hats break in without permission for gain, revenge or harm - ransomware crews and credit-card thieves. White hats use identical skills with written permission to find and fix weaknesses - hired penetration testers. Gray hats mean well but skip the permission, reporting holes they had no right to find, sometimes for a fee - helpful intent, illegal act. Script kiddies are unskilled attackers running others' tools - low sophistication, real damage in numbers. Hacktivists hack for political or social causes - defacements and leaks as protest. State-sponsored hackers work for governments on espionage and sabotage - Stuxnet at Natanz is the reference example. Cybercriminals are black hats organized as businesses - financially motivated, structured like companies.

Close with the hat origin: the colors come from Western films, and the map that orders them is permission against intent - white sits at permitted and helpful, black at unpermitted and harmful, gray in between.

questions.question: What is penetration testing? Explain its types and phases.
questions.answer:
Definition first: a focused, controlled, authorized simulation of a cyberattack on a specific system to identify and exploit vulnerabilities - scoped, ruled, permitted, and proven rather than assumed.

Types come in two families. By knowledge: black box (nothing known - the external stranger), gray box (partial knowledge - the insider or phished account), white box (everything known - source code and configs, deepest audit). By target: external (the perimeter), internal (the insider threat, privilege escalation and lateral movement), web application (SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, authentication flaws), wireless (encryption and rogue access points), and social engineering (the human perimeter: phishing, pretexting, baiting).

Phases mirror the hacking lifecycle under contract: planning and reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, maintaining access, analysis and reporting. Close with the tools: Metasploit for exploitation, Nmap for scanning, Burp Suite for web, Wireshark for traffic, John the Ripper for passwords, Nikto and OWASP ZAP for web scanning, Dmitry for reconnaissance.

questions.question: Explain Nmap and its main features, with the commands used in the lab.
questions.answer:
Definition: Nmap (Network Mapper) is a free, open-source tool for network discovery and security auditing - it discovers live hosts, open ports, and the services and operating systems behind them. Published by Fyodor in Phrack in 1997, it remains the standard scanner for administrators and attackers alike.

Features: host discovery (ping sweeps across a range), port scanning with three reported states (open, closed, filtered), service and version detection (-sV), OS fingerprinting (-O, reading TTL, window size, DF and TOS habits), the Nmap Scripting Engine for vulnerability detection, stealth techniques like the SYN half-open scan (-sS), and full network mapping.

Lab commands: nmap <target> scans the 1000 common ports; -F the fastest 100; -p picks ports exactly, by list, range or service name; -A runs the aggressive all-in-one scan; a /24 suffix scans the whole subnet; -O detects the OS. Close with the legal line: scanning without authorization is illegal; practice targets like scanme.nmap.org and testphp.vulweb.com exist for exactly this purpose.

questions.question: Describe the ethical principles an ethical hacker must follow.
questions.answer:
Open with the frame: the tools of a white hat and a black hat are identical, so what makes hacking ethical is a code of conduct, not a technique.

Legality: explicit written permission and compliance with the law (IT Act 2000 in India). Confidentiality: protect everything sensitive seen during the test, usually bound by an NDA. Integrity: honest, complete reporting and no conflicts of interest. Non-malfeasance: do no harm - minimize risk, work in agreed windows, stop at unforeseen danger. Responsibility: own and be able to justify every action. Transparency: communicate scope, methods, risks and results openly. Professionalism: keep learning as threats evolve.

Close: break any one principle and the tester becomes legally indistinguishable from the attacker they imitate.

questions.question: Compare passive and active reconnaissance, with tools for each.
questions.answer:
Definitions: reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase. Passive reconnaissance collects from public sources without contacting the target - WHOIS lookups, Google dorking, Shodan, company sites, social media, Netcraft (via Dmitry -n). Because nothing is sent to the target, nothing can be logged: the phase is invisible, but limited to what is already public.

Active reconnaissance interacts with the target directly - ping sweeps, port scans (Nmap, Dmitry -p), banner grabbing (Dmitry -b). It learns far more - live hosts, open ports, running services - at the price of visibility: packets arrive and can be logged or alarmed.

The professional sequence is passive first, active second: shrink the target list silently, then spend your noise budget only where it pays. Dmitry demonstrates both halves in one tool, which is exactly why your lecturer chose it for the reconnaissance lab.

questions.question: Is port scanning legal? Discuss with reference to practice targets.
questions.answer:
The act of scanning is identical either way; the legality turns entirely on authorization. Scanning systems you own or have written permission to test is a professional service and a routine administrative act. Scanning systems without permission is unauthorized probing of someone else's property - illegal in most jurisdictions, including India under the Information Technology Act 2000, and visible in server logs besides.

The gray zones students ask about: scanning is rarely prosecuted when it is trivial background noise, but "rarely prosecuted" is not "legal", and intent cannot be proven after the fact. The professional rule is simple - permission first, in writing.

Practice targets remove every excuse: scanme.nmap.org is run by the Nmap project explicitly for scanning practice; testphp.vulweb.com is a deliberately vulnerable site built to be attacked; and a virtual machine lab on your own machine is entirely yours. Skill is built on legal targets or not at all.

questions.question: How does a vulnerability become a breach? Trace the life of a flaw.
questions.answer:
A vulnerability is born when flawed code or configuration ships - the developer does not know, and neither does anyone else. If an attacker finds it first, it becomes a zero-day: exploited while the vendor has had zero days to fix it, the most dangerous state a flaw can have.

Once the vendor learns of it, a race begins: the vendor writes a patch while attackers scale up exploitation of everyone unpatched. The flaw gets a public ID (a CVE number), scanners like Nessus learn to detect it, and frameworks like Metasploit package the exploit. From that day the vulnerability is known - and every unpatched machine is a sitting target, because the attack now costs the attacker nothing.

Equifax 2017 is the closing argument: the Apache Struts flaw had a public patch for two months, the patch was not applied, and 147 million records were lost. The lifecycle lesson: the danger window is not closed by the patch existing - only by the patch being applied, which is why the hacking lifecycle ends in remediation and retesting, not in the report.

questions.question: nmap -F 199.59.243.227
questions.answer: Fast scan of the 100 most common ports on that IP. The quick "is anything obviously exposed?" check.

questions.question: nmap -p 1-15,20-25 199.59.243.227
questions.answer: Scans two port ranges: 1 to 15 and 20 to 25. -p accepts ranges and mixes them with commas.

questions.question: nmap -p mysql,https,ftp 199.59.243.227
questions.answer: Scans by service name instead of number - Nmap translates mysql, https and ftp to 3306, 443 and 21. For when you remember the service, not the port.

questions.question: nmap -A www.gmail.com
questions.answer: Aggressive scan: OS detection, version detection, script scanning and traceroute in one run. Loud, slow, thorough.

questions.question: nmap 192.168.127.1/24
questions.answer: Scans all 256 addresses of the subnet - the ping sweep that discovers every device on the local network.

questions.question: nmap -O 199.59.243.1
questions.answer: OS detection: fingerprints the operating system from its TCP/IP habits (TTL, window size, DF, TOS).

questions.question: dmitry -wsepn www.google.com
questions.answer: One passive-recon barrage: domain whois, subdomains, emails, port scan and Netcraft info, saved in one run - flags combine freely.

questions.question: nikto -h www.github.com
questions.answer: Web server vulnerability scan against the named host - missing security headers, dangerous files, known flaws. Noisy by nature; expect it in the logs.
